newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan finance workers worried by Big Bang--survey.
newsitem.headline: Japan finance workers worried by Big Bang--survey.

text.p: Most employees of Japanese financial institutions are worried about the future of their firms because of looming "Big Bang" reforms, a survey by the economic journal Nihon Keizai Shimbun showed on Tuesday.

The survey of 636 workers at banks, insurance firms and securities houses showed that 72 percent of respondents were worried their companies' management might not be able to survive the reforms, the paper said.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has staked much of his reputation as a reformer on the deregulation of financial institutions, which he announced last November, modelled on the City of London's 1986 "Big Bang".
The reforms are due to be completed by 2001 to bring Japan into line with practices of other major financial centres.

About 57 percent of respondents to the survey, which was carried out from July 9 to 22, said foreign financial firms had better know-how of high-quality financial products and could make quicker managerial decisions than Japanese firms.

In recent years, high costs and unwieldy regulations have triggered an exodus of foreign financial institutions from Japan. Many have moved their Asian headquarters to more open and less costly centres such as Singapore or Hong Kong.

But foreign firms, more adept at competing in a deregulated environment and equipped with products that are in hot demand, stand a good chance this time of overwhelming their Japanese counterparts, officials of many foreign firms say.

More than 93 percent of respondents to the newspaper survey said a recent scandal involving top Japanese securities houses did not represent a new trend. Ninety percent said the firms involved were not alone and similar problems haunted all Japanese financial companies.

The Ministry of Finance imposed sanctions on one of Japan's top commercial banks, Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB), and giant brokerage Nomura Securities Co Ltd on July 30 in connection with a high-profile scandal involving payoffs to a corporate racketeer.
Prosecutors also raided Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd on July 30 in search of evidence of alleged payoffs to Ryuichi Koike, the racketeer at the heart of the Nomura-DKB scandal.
